title: Foundry-made fault-tolerant quantum computation without a dilution refrigerator

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a universal quantum processor made using industrial foundry processes that can protect and manipulate its logical quantum information without keeping its computational qubits at millikelvin temperatures. Fault tolerance means that increasing the protection provided by error correction can reduce logical errors sufficiently to support longer computations. Foundry fabrication must deliver components with the required performance reliably; making an individual chip in a foundry does not establish the complete capability. Photonics provides a concrete route because most computational components can operate at room temperature, although optical loss remains a major obstacle.

There are two distinct thermal boundaries. Keeping the computational modes warm is the narrower goal. The title's strict interpretation additionally excludes a dilution refrigerator needed elsewhere to supply indispensable computational resources. Cryogenic detectors that herald successful preparation of input states can remain essential to the computer even when they sit outside its warm processing unit. A machine dependent on such dilution-refrigerator-based preparation would therefore fall short of the strict version.

significance.text: If achieved, this combination would change the physical infrastructure required for universal fault-tolerant computation: industrial fabrication would be combined with computational qubits that need no millikelvin stage. The strict version would also remove dilution-refrigerator dependence from resource-state preparation. This would eliminate a substantial thermal requirement and could make processors easier to reproduce, integrate and deploy. The significance is an enabling change in how quantum computers are manufactured and operated, rather than a new computational model.

Warm computation and foundry fabrication would not by themselves make these machines affordable for ordinary laboratories. Manufacturing yield, packaging, component uniformity, control equipment and error-correction overhead would still determine practical accessibility. Aurora's paper illustrates the scale of this challenge with a projected 100-logical-qubit configuration whose state factory could require tens of thousands of server racks, even under substantial assumed improvements. That estimate is not an unavoidable lower bound for future designs, but it prevents treating widespread laboratory ownership as an automatic consequence of removing millikelvin cooling.

A photonic implementation also has a demonstrated technical basis for connecting modules through optical fibre. Higher clock rates are a possible engineering benefit, rather than an established consequence of this concept. Networking functionality must still be distinguished from interconnects that preserve fault tolerance at useful scale.

Conditional synthesis: useful cryptographic and scientific workloads would still require enough logical qubits, sufficiently accurate operations and feasible execution times. Removing refrigeration does not establish those application capabilities or guarantee a quantum speedup. Conversely, if refrigerated machines become inexpensive and widely available, the relative accessibility advantage of this innovation could shrink, although its manufacturing and thermal distinctions would remain.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability in the documented Aurora result is the integration of foundry fabrication, warm computational modes and distance-scalable universal fault tolerance. Demonstrating components, connecting modules or running a small error-correction circuit does not establish that combination. Both protected storage and the logical operations needed for universal computation must have errors that can be suppressed through error correction.

For the optical route, loss must be reduced throughout state preparation, heralding, routing and computation while other relevant errors remain compatible with fault tolerance. Aurora's reported losses were approximately 56% on heralding paths and slightly over 95% on heralded optical paths, compared with loss budgets around 1% for the configurations analysed in the paper. These quantities concern different paths and should not be collapsed into one device-wide loss figure. The approximately 1% budgets are architecture-dependent attainable benchmarks from explicit constructions, rather than a universal threshold or a proven hard upper limit.

The barriers extend beyond optical transmission. State preparation, detection, adaptive control and universal computational resources must function together under a realistic joint noise model. The paper left verification of how magic-state generation affects loss tolerance to further work. Component performance must also survive mass production and system integration. A design that works only with exceptional components, or requires impractically large resource factories, would leave major engineering barriers unresolved.

Under the strict thermal requirement, indispensable dilution-refrigerator-dependent heralding must be replaced or eliminated while preserving the quality and supply rate of computational resource states. Moving that apparatus outside the processing unit does not remove the dependency. Aurora documents the distinction between room-temperature computational operations and cryogenic input preparation; it does not demonstrate the required replacement.

current_state.text: Published on 22 January 2025 in Nature, R. Baby, H. Chen and collaborators' “Scaling and networking a modular photonic quantum computer” reported Aurora as a scale model demonstrating integrated modular photonic-computing functionality, with performance insufficient for fault tolerance. It established a relevant architectural route and working system integration, while making universal fault-tolerant computation conditional on improved components.

Aurora implemented a distance-2 repetition-code experiment with real-time decoding and adaptive operation. The system was too noisy to demonstrate error suppression. The experiment therefore demonstrated building blocks and their coordination, without showing that larger codes reduce logical error or that a universal set of logical operations operates below threshold.

The paper's Discussion and outlook reported approximately 56% loss on heralding paths and slightly over 95% on heralded paths, against approximately 1% loss budgets for the fault-tolerant configurations considered. This was a substantial performance gap at publication. The figures describe the analysed architecture and paths; they do not establish a universal photonic loss limit. The authors also identified the effect of magic-state generation on loss tolerance as requiring further verification.

Aurora's source chips were fabricated on X-Fab Silicon Foundries SE's 200-mm production manufacturing line. This supports industrial foundry provenance for those chips, rather than a demonstration of a complete foundry-made fault-tolerant processor. Most components operated at room temperature, but the photon-number-resolving detection system used two Bluefors LD400 dilution refrigerators with a 12-mK base temperature. In the optical Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill, or GKP, approach described by the paper, cryogenic detection heralds certain prepared input states. Aurora consequently did not demonstrate independence from dilution refrigeration for the whole system.

The supplied review assessed saved HTML and PDF copies containing the article and Methods, with no indicated extraction truncation. Supplementary material and figure images were not supplied for inspection; the reviewed findings rely on explicit prose rather than independent interpretation of plots. The supplied record contains no bounded search establishing subsequent field-wide progress through 1 November 2026. It therefore supports the dated Aurora findings, but cannot establish that the proposed capability remains unachieved across the field on that later date. It also provides no inspected evidence supporting the earlier Willow comparison. These limitations do not invalidate Aurora's reported results.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a processor fabricated through commercial foundry processes, document its manufacturing provenance and thermal dependencies, and show logical error decreasing over multiple increasing code distances under comparable operating conditions. Demonstrate a set of logical operations sufficient for universal computation, with errors that can be suppressed through error correction. A successful memory experiment alone, or an unprotected universal physical gate set, would not satisfy this proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Universal foundry logical operations whose error falls with code distance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed noise evaluation: assess loss, gate errors, state preparation, measurement, adaptive control and relevant correlations jointly against the chosen architecture's fault-tolerance conditions. Report operating assumptions and measured margins, rather than applying approximately 1% loss as a universal pass/fail rule. The Aurora paper's explicit constructions motivate architecture-specific evaluation, but these completion requirements are proposals rather than established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Joint noise margins and assumptions against architecture fault-tolerance conditions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed thermal demonstration: verify that computational qubits require no millikelvin stage. For the strict title-level claim, additionally show that no indispensable resource-state preparation, heralding or other supporting operation depends on a dilution refrigerator. Merely locating cryogenic detectors outside the warm processor would not meet that boundary. This requirement concerns dilution refrigeration; it does not silently impose an additional requirement that every component operate at room temperature.
completion_criteria.label: Millikelvin-free computational qubits and dilution-refrigerator-independent indispensable support

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical evaluation: repeat the result across devices and fabrication runs, report component yield and variation, and enable independent reproduction of the central logical-error and thermal-dependency findings. Disclose resource-state throughput, factory size, packaging and control requirements, runtime and operating footprint. A compact laboratory installation need not be a prerequisite for demonstrating the core capability, but evidence of affordable deployment would require separate support. Finite experiments can establish performance across tested circuits, code sizes and conditions; they cannot empirically prove success for every circuit or arbitrary computation length.
completion_criteria.label: Cross-fabrication reproduction of logical-error and thermal findings with operating requirements

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: QUA-01, “Distance-scalable universal fault-tolerant quantum computation,” supplies the central computational capability also required here. QUA-10 adds industrial foundry fabrication and a thermal infrastructure constraint. Improved fidelity, longer coherence or more physical qubits are useful components, but do not alone complete either system-level goal. A seconds-to-minutes room-temperature coherence target would likewise be a component objective, not a substitute for universal logical fault tolerance.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-02, “Cryptographically relevant execution of Shor’s algorithm,” and QUA-03, “Experimentally confirmed quantum prediction of sign-problematic matter,” concern application achievements. A QUA-10 processor could provide hardware for them, but would still need the required logical scale, accuracy and execution resources. Neither application requires this particular manufacturing or thermal route merely by definition.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-04 concerns a material that stores a logical qubit passively at nonzero temperature. Passive storage differs from actively executing universal fault-tolerant computation, and nonzero temperature does not necessarily mean room temperature. Such a material might contribute to QUA-10 if it could be integrated into a suitable processor. QUA-05 concerns universal computation by braiding non-Abelian anyons, a specific computational mechanism that does not by itself establish foundry compatibility or freedom from dilution refrigeration.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-06 concerns fault-tolerant interconnects that support scaling by adding modules. It overlaps the networking needs of a modular photonic QUA-10 implementation, while Aurora's modular functionality alone does not establish that interconnect capability. QUA-08 concerns local universal fault tolerance with bounded overhead as errors fall. Better overhead could materially improve QUA-10's practical footprint, but its overhead condition is distinct from QUA-10's fabrication and thermal requirements.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-07 is a mathematical separation between quantum and classical polynomial-time decision computation, rather than a hardware achievement. QUA-09 requires an end-to-end superpolynomial speedup on large classical data, including the costs of accessing and processing those data. A foundry-made processor without dilution refrigeration would not itself prove either result. These distinctions follow from the supplied roster titles; full records for the other concepts were not provided.

The impact of magic-state generation on the analysed architecture's loss tolerance remained for further verification in the supplied paper.
The supplied evidence does not identify a demonstrated replacement for Aurora's dilution-refrigerator-dependent input-state heralding.
Achievable manufacturing yield, packaging reliability, resource overhead and deployment cost for a completed system remain undetermined.

brief.title: Factory-made quantum computers without ultracold fridges
possible: Researchers could run longer, error-protected quantum calculations on processors made in commercial chip factories. Stronger error correction would make calculations more reliable, without requiring the deepest cooling either in the processor or in equipment essential to feeding it.
why: This would change how quantum computers are manufactured and operated. Combining industrial chip production with less demanding cooling could make processors easier to reproduce, connect and deploy.

sources.showed: They built Aurora, a light-based quantum computer that connected chip modules and ran a small error-correction experiment with immediate responses to measurements.
sources.quote: Here we construct a (sub-performant) scale model of a quantum computer using 35 photonic chips to demonstrate its functionality and feasibility.
sources.cited_for: Aurora demonstrated that the main computing components could work together.
sources.not_established: Its errors were too large to demonstrate increasing protection, and essential detectors still required ultracold refrigeration.

sources.showed: They built factory-made chips that generated, manipulated, connected and detected quantum bits carried by light. Their accuracy measurements excluded lost photons.
sources.quote:
Using this stack, we build quantum photonic integrated circuits 
using standard silicon photonic waveguide components, including 
directional couplers, crossings and thermal phase shifters.
sources.cited_for: Commercial chip manufacturing can integrate key components for light-based quantum computing.
sources.not_established: The components did not demonstrate a complete error-protected computer, and their integrated detectors required cooling.

sources.showed: They generated GKP states, patterns of light that encode quantum bits and resist certain errors, using an integrated chip and photon-counting detectors.
sources.quote: Here we report the synthesis and characterization of optical GKP qubit states in the 1,550-nm wavelength band.
sources.cited_for: Integrated chips can produce a type of light state needed by Aurora's computing approach.
sources.not_established: The states still needed lower optical losses to support error-protected computation.

sources.showed: In a preprint, simulations found that failed attempts to join light-based quantum states can limit accuracy at fixed protection size, even without photon loss.
sources.quote:
We show that in this regime, fusion failure imposes a noise
floor on the logical error rate that prevents all-linear-optics architectures from reaching the required
rates at low overhead.
sources.cited_for: A tolerable photon-loss rate alone does not establish practical error-protected computing.
sources.not_established: The simulations examined selected designs rather than demonstrating a working processor.

shown: Aurora combined most components at room temperature with factory-made source chips. PsiQuantum demonstrated integrated manufacturing, while Larsen and collaborators produced needed light states. These were system and component demonstrations; none demonstrated the complete capability.
missing: A factory-made processor must perform general-purpose quantum operations whose errors fall as protection increases.
Photon loss and other errors must remain low enough when preparation, control, measurement and computation operate together.
Essential input preparation must work without a dilution refrigerator, the equipment used to reach temperatures near absolute zero.
Performance must survive repeated manufacturing runs, with measured production yield and operating requirements.

milestones.label: Factory-made calculations improve with stronger protection
milestones.explanation: A factory-made processor would have to show falling errors as protection grows, for operations sufficient for general-purpose quantum computation. This would establish reliable computing beyond protected storage.

milestones.label: Combined errors stay within the design's tolerance
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to assess loss, operation errors, preparation, measurement, control and linked errors together, stating assumptions and safety margins. This would test whether the whole design can sustain error correction.

milestones.label: Computation and essential support avoid ultracold refrigeration
milestones.explanation: Quantum bits would have to operate without cooling close to absolute zero, with no essential support depending on a dilution refrigerator. This would establish independence from that cooling throughout the computer.

milestones.label: Repeated production preserves reliability and cooling independence
milestones.explanation: Devices from separate production runs would have to reproduce the findings independently, with yield, variation, input supply, equipment, runtime and footprint reported. This would establish repeatability and deployment requirements.

uncertain: How preparing the special input states needed for general-purpose computation affects tolerable photon loss remains unresolved.
Manufacturing consistency, packaging reliability, equipment size and deployment cost remain undetermined.
Passing error limits does not settle how much hardware a useful calculation would require; that depends on the design.

page.title: Foundry-made fault-tolerant quantum computing without dilution cooling
page.definition: A processor fabricated in a semiconductor foundry performs error-corrected operations sufficient to approximate any quantum circuit. Increasing the error correction suppresses logical errors. The photonic approaches encode a qubit in the two paths available to one photon or in a grid in the optical field of a single mode. The qubits require no millikelvin stage, and every essential step, from preparing the qubits to reading the answer, works without dilution refrigeration. Detectors cooled to a few kelvin are compatible with this requirement. Aurora illustrates the distinction: its optical processor used photon counters housed in two dilution refrigerators at a base temperature of 12 mK.

goal.need: Ammonia production uses about 2% of global final energy. Chemists want to understand how nitrogenase makes ammonia at room temperature. Classical methods already give an accurate ground-state energy for one model of its active site. Quantum calculations could distinguish reaction pathways whose energies remain beyond classical reach. Long calculations require many qubits and low logical error rates. Foundries can make optical components in volume, and detectors operating a few degrees above absolute zero can use industrial helium plants with kilowatts of cooling power.

figures.caption: Optical-loss gap reported for Aurora on 22 January 2025
figures.note: The paths differ. The budgets depend on the analysed architecture; 1% is not a universal photonic threshold.

The academy was assessing PsiQuantum’s six-year timetable for addressing photon loss, generation, routing, coupling and detection. It also questioned the cryogenic power demand if it grew linearly with the number of logical qubits.

completion.title: A foundry-made processor performs universal fault-tolerant computation without dilution refrigeration.
completion.criterion: A processor fabricated through commercial semiconductor-foundry processes executes a universal logical gate set while increased error correction suppresses errors in storage and logical operations. Its measured loss and other noise satisfy the implemented architecture’s fault-tolerance conditions, including state preparation and measurement. Computational qubits require no millikelvin stage, and no indispensable state preparation, heralding, detection, control or interconnect depends on a dilution refrigerator.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis; no external acceptance test found for the combined capability.
completion.basis: Searches of IEEE’s quantum-standards catalogue, ISO/IEC 4879’s public scope, DARPA US2QC goals, and PsiQuantum and Xanadu publications and roadmaps found no combined foundry, fault-tolerance and refrigeration test. This criterion joins the accuracy-threshold convention to the developers’ manufacturing and cooling statements. It adds no numerical yield, footprint or universal loss target.

milestones.title: Foundry-made photonic modules generate, manipulate, detect and network qubits.
milestones.criterion: Modules made in a commercial semiconductor foundry demonstrate qubit generation, manipulation, detection and chip-to-chip interconnection in the chosen encoding. For the dual-rail protocol, measure state preparation and readout, interference between independent photon sources, two-qubit fusion and transfer between chips. Report which measurements are conditioned on photon detection.
milestones.set_by: PsiQuantum’s published module-benchmark protocol in Nature; demonstrated with dual-rail photonic qubits.
milestones.threshold_quote: demonstrating the crucial functionalities of qubit generation, manipulation, detection and networking

milestones.title: A photonic processor decodes error information and conditions its next computational operation.
milestones.criterion: During execution, decode the measured error information and use the inferred recovery to select the computational operation at the next time step.
milestones.set_by: Xanadu’s Aurora experimental protocol in Nature; written for optical GKP processing.
milestones.threshold_quote: running a decoder in real time, and performing a conditional operation at the following time step based on the recovery.

milestones.title: An error-corrected photonic qubit has a memory-lifetime ratio greater than 1.
milestones.criterion: Under repeated error correction, the lifetime of an arbitrary encoded qubit exceeds that of the best corresponding unencoded physical qubit. The corrected-to-unencoded lifetime ratio must exceed 1 when the comparison includes correction overhead and tests preservation of quantum information without postselection.
milestones.set_by: Quantum-memory break-even convention, explicitly defined by Ofek and colleagues in Nature; originally demonstrated in superconducting circuits.
milestones.threshold_quote: at which the lifetime of a qubit exceeds the lifetime of the constituents of the system

milestones.title: A photonic memory’s logical-error suppression factor exceeds 1 as its error-correcting code grows.
milestones.criterion: At fixed physical operating conditions, measure logical memory error per correction cycle at increasing code sizes. The decrease must be consistent with exponential suppression, with a fitted logical-error suppression factor greater than 1.
milestones.set_by: Below-threshold error-correction convention, demonstrated by Google Quantum AI; its reported experiment used superconducting surface-code memories.
milestones.threshold_quote: However, this exponential suppression only occurs if the physical error rate is below a critical threshold.

milestones.title: A photonic processor executes universal logical gates below its architecture’s fault-tolerance threshold.
milestones.criterion: A photonic processor implements encoded preparation, measurement and a universal logical gate set, including entangling and non-Clifford operations. Their errors can be suppressed by increasing error correction under the architecture’s joint noise model, including photon loss and resource-state preparation. Universal means that the operations can approximate any quantum circuit. This establishes the computational capability before its integration with the foundry and thermal conditions in the completion test.
milestones.set_by: Quantum accuracy-threshold convention of Knill, Laflamme and Zurek, together with the universal logical-gate requirement exemplified by Postler and colleagues; the latter experiment used trapped ions.
milestones.threshold_quote: Here we show that arbitrarily accurate quantum computations are possible provided that the error per operation is below a threshold value.

milestones.title: An optical source prepares a qubit and measurements verify its encoding.
milestones.criterion: Prepare a qubit in the chosen optical encoding and measure the output state. For dual rail, prepare and measure a heralded single photon in two optical paths. For an optical GKP source, measure both field quadratures and reconstruct the state to resolve its grid structure.
milestones.set_by: The state-preparation and measurement protocols of the PsiQuantum dual-rail and Larsen optical GKP experiments.
milestones.threshold_quote: the synthesis and characterization of optical GKP qubit states

milestones.title: Single-photon detectors read out photonic qubits without dilution refrigeration.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate qubit readout with the required single-photon detectors operating on a cooling system that uses no dilution refrigerator. Identify the cooling system and the detector operating temperature. PsiQuantum’s detector design calls for operation a few degrees above absolute zero.
milestones.set_by: PsiQuantum’s detector operating condition for its collaboration with SLAC.
milestones.threshold_quote: These single-photon detectors operate at temperatures a few degrees above absolute zero.

milestones.title: Measured photon loss falls within the budget for the chosen optical circuit and code.
milestones.criterion: Measure optical loss and compare it with the loss allowance for the implemented circuit under the assumptions used to derive that allowance. For Aurora’s GKP design, compare the three principal path losses jointly at the specified combined tree depth. For the (2,2)-Shor-encoded six-ring fusion network with Bell-pair boosting and 25% fusion failure, the model requires less than 2.7% independent loss per photon. Use the corresponding budget when the circuit or noise assumptions differ.
milestones.set_by: The Aurora path-loss analysis and the fusion-network loss model of Bartolucci and colleagues.
milestones.threshold_quote: With the 25% failure probability achieved with fusions boosted with a Bell pair, we have a loss tolerance of 2.7% per photon.

results.finding: Aurora’s heralded squeezed-cat precursors accounted for 3.05% of the modes in the repetition-code experiment.
results.detail: When heralding failed, the multiplexer selected a squeezed state. The separate two-quadrature entanglement benchmark used Gaussian states.
results.quote: On failure to observe two photons, a squeezed state is selected by the multiplexer, so that the resulting cluster-state modes are in a combination of squeezed states and squeezed cat states—the latter make up 3.05% on average of the modes.

results.finding: Aurora’s 35-chip modular processor synthesized and measured a Gaussian cluster state spanning 86.4 billion modes.
results.detail: The source chips were fabricated at X-Fab. The Gaussian benchmark bypassed photon-number detection. In the adaptive run, photon counts conditioned precursor selection, with squeezed states used when heralding failed.
results.quote: Continuously acquired over 2 hours, this result represents the synthesis and measurement of a macronode cluster state consisting of 86.4 billion modes, or 86.4/12 = 7.2 billion temporal modes.

results.finding: Aurora used real-time repetition-code decoding to select the next measurement basis, with approximately 976 ns of signal-chain latency over 13.8 million decoding repetitions.
results.detail: The cluster mixed squeezed states with low-quality GKP precursors. A randomized-basis control tested whether the observed correlations depended on decoder-driven feedforward.
results.quote: The full signal chain latency from an optical pulse arriving at the homodyne detectors to the actuation of an updated local oscillator phase is approximately 976 ns.

results.finding: Aurora’s 35-chip prototype showed about 56% loss on its photon-heralding path.
results.detail: The modeled joint allowance applies to the proposed full GKP state factory. Aurora’s refinery performed multiplexing and entanglement but lacked the breeding stage in that design.
results.quote: Aurora shows losses of about 56% for the heralding paths

results.finding: A heralded optical GKP |1⟩ state reconstructed from about 1.9 million quadrature measurements showed a 3 × 3 grid of negative Wigner regions.
results.detail: Tomography was conditioned on the (3, 3, 3) photon-count pattern after discarding the noisiest 20% of outcomes from each photon-number-resolving detector. State reconstruction used no loss compensation.
results.quote: here we see our state achieves a 3 × 3 grid of negative Wigner regions.

results.finding: One chip fabricated on a 300-mm silicon nitride wafer generated heralded optical GKP qubits verified by homodyne tomography.

results.quote: Here we use an ultra-low-loss integrated photonic chip fabricated on a customized multilayer silicon nitride 300-mm wafer platform, coupled over fibre with high-efficiency photon number resolving detectors, to generate GKP qubit states.

definition = "A processor fabricated in a semiconductor foundry performs error-corrected operations sufficient to approximate any quantum circuit. Increasing the error correction suppresses logical errors. The photonic approaches encode a qubit in the two paths available to one photon or in a grid in the optical field of a single mode. The qubits require no millikelvin stage, and every essential step, from preparing the qubits to reading the answer, works without dilution refrigeration. Detectors cooled to a few kelvin are compatible with this requirement. Aurora illustrates the distinction: its optical processor used photon counters housed in two dilution refrigerators at a base temperature of 12 mK.". Reason: The definition leaves the optical encodings unexplained and does not show why a processor with room-temperature optics can still depend on a dilution refrigerator.

goal.need = "Ammonia production uses about 2% of global final energy. Chemists want to understand how nitrogenase makes ammonia at room temperature. Classical methods already give an accurate ground-state energy for one model of its active site. Quantum calculations could distinguish reaction pathways whose energies remain beyond classical reach. Long calculations require many qubits and low logical error rates. Foundries can make optical components in volume, and detectors operating a few degrees above absolute zero can use industrial helium plants with kilowatts of cooling power.". Reason: The current rationale describes two machines without explaining what a user could calculate, what classical methods already achieve or why the cooling temperature matters.

add statement by PsiQuantum, 2023: "to prove the viability of existing cryogenic cooling solutions to support building a large-scale, error-corrected quantum computer.". Reason: The project’s own statement identifies the purpose of its cooling work and allows the claim to be attached to the detector design it describes.

add statement by Australian and Queensland governments, 2024: "to build a groundbreaking utility-scale fault tolerant quantum computer (FTQC) in Australia.". Reason: The Australian and Queensland governments committed to building a specific machine beyond the evaluation goal already attributed to DARPA.

add statement by Académie des technologies, France, 2025: "which seems rather optimistic.". Reason: The academy’s assessment supplies an independent judgment about the feasibility of the published schedule.

add milestone after None: "An optical source prepares a qubit and measurements verify its encoding.". Reason: A verified qubit source is an independently demonstrated laboratory step that precedes the four-function foundry benchmark.

edit m1: criterion = "Modules made in a commercial semiconductor foundry demonstrate qubit generation, manipulation, detection and chip-to-chip interconnection in the chosen encoding. For the dual-rail protocol, measure state preparation and readout, interference between independent photon sources, two-qubit fusion and transfer between chips. Report which measurements are conditioned on photon detection.". Reason: The criterion mixes dated results with the test and leaves readers to infer which operations the dual-rail benchmark measures.

add milestone after m1: "Single-photon detectors read out photonic qubits without dilution refrigeration.". Reason: The existing component benchmarks allow dilution-cooled detectors, so they leave the thermal requirement untested until completion.

edit m2: criterion = "During execution, decode the measured error information and use the inferred recovery to select the computational operation at the next time step.". Reason: The Aurora result belongs with the evidence, while the criterion needs only the real-time decision and its deadline.

add milestone after m2: "Measured photon loss falls within the budget for the chosen optical circuit and code.". Reason: High fidelities conditioned on detecting a photon leave open whether the optical circuit loses too many photons for its error-correcting code.

edit m3: criterion = "Under repeated error correction, the lifetime of an arbitrary encoded qubit exceeds that of the best corresponding unencoded physical qubit. The corrected-to-unencoded lifetime ratio must exceed 1 when the comparison includes correction overhead and tests preservation of quantum information without postselection.". Reason: The superconducting-resonator result is already identified in the attribution and does not belong in the photonic acceptance test.

edit m4: criterion = "At fixed physical operating conditions, measure logical memory error per correction cycle at increasing code sizes. The decrease must be consistent with exponential suppression, with a fitted logical-error suppression factor greater than 1."; refs = [11]. Reason: The existing criterion includes a fixed-code-size simulation even though the test requires measured logical errors as code size increases.

add not found: "No study located quantified ammonia-production energy savings attributable to a fault-tolerant calculation of nitrogen fixation.". Reason: The industrial energy figure measures the scale of ammonia production and cannot serve as an estimate of the benefit of a quantum calculation.
remove statement 1. Reason: The 2023 quotation generalizes a cooling claim about PsiQuantum’s detectors to photonic architectures that include Aurora’s dilution-cooled design.
